extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of Euclidean geometry (advanced high-school / undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted chapter (Book VI) of Euclid on similarity, proportion, and constructions: definitions, theorems, problems, corollaries and exercises about similar rectilineal figures, proportional lines, mean proportionals, and area ratios. Useful for learning or teaching classical synthetic geometry and for constructing proportional segments and similar figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: If three magnitudes be continual proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: If three magnitudes be continual proportionals, the first is to the third as the square of the difference between the first and second is to the square of the difference between the second and third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of a proportional identity relating three continual proportionals and squares of differences; no full proof in this chunk, but it is given as a proposition-style assertion (useful as an algebraic/geometric relation among terms in geometric progression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic-bisected-line proportionalities (items 9–13)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. If a line AB, cut harmonically in C and D, be bisected in O; prove OC, OB, OD are continual proportionals. 10. In the same case, if O' be the middle point of CD; prove OO'² = OB² + O'D². 11. And AB(AC+AD) = 2 AC·AD, or + = . 12. And CD(AD+BD) = 2 AD·BD, or + = . 13. And AB·CD = 2 AD·CB·(???).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collection of related statements about harmonic division, bisectors, mean proportionals and algebraic relations among segments produced by harmonic division and bisectors. They serve as small theorems/exercises illustrating properties of harmonic division and relations between segments; proofs use previous proportionality results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition i — Similar Rectilineal Figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar Rectilineal Figures are those whose several angles are equal, each to each, and whose sides about the equal angles are proportional. Similar figures agree in shape; if they agree also in size, they are congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the working definition of similarity: equality of corresponding angles and proportionality of corresponding sides. Distinguishes species (shape), magnitude (size), and position. Useful for judging when two polygons/figures are 'similar'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition ii — Extreme and mean ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: A right line is said to be cut at a point in extreme and mean ratio when the whole line is to the greater segment as the greater segment is to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the classical 'extreme and mean ratio' (golden-section style) used in constructions and characterization of harmonic division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition iii — Mean proportional / geometrical progression
rubrics_metrics.description: If three quantities of the same kind be in continued proportion, the middle term is called a mean proportional between the other two. Magnitudes in continued proportion are also said to be in geometrical progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for mean proportional (geometric mean) used repeatedly in subsequent propositions and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition iv — Two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: If four quantities of the same kind be in continued proportion, the two middle terms are called two mean proportionals between the other two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for the case of two successive mean proportionals (useful for cube-root style constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition v — Altitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The altitude of any figure is the length of the perpendicular from its highest point to its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of altitude as perpendicular distance; used in area relations in later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition vi — Reciprocal proportionality of sides about corresponding angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Two corresponding angles of two figures have the sides about them reciprocally proportional, when a side of the first is to a side of the second as the remaining side of the second is to the remaining side of the first. This is equivalent to saying that a side of the first is to a side of the second in the reciprocal ratio of the remaining side of the first to the remaining side of the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives notion of reciprocal proportionality of adjacent sides about corresponding equal angles; appears in proofs relating parallelograms/triangles equalities and area relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I — Triangles and parallelograms with same altitude are as their bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles (ABC, ACD) and parallelograms (EC, CF) which have the same altitude are to one another as their bases (BC, CD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses equimultiples and equality of triangles on equal bases with same altitude; also provides alternate area-based proof using area = altitude × base. Corollary: parallelograms equal in altitude compare as their bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II — Parallel line divides sides proportionally (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line (DE) be parallel to a side (BC) of a triangle (ABC), it divides the remaining sides, measured from the opposite angle (A), proportionally; and, conversely, If two sides of a triangle, measured from an angle, be cut proportionally, the line joining the points of section is parallel to the third side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives both forward and converse statements; proof uses triangles on same base and between same parallels; observation notes the line DE may cut produced sides and similar figures cover those cases. Exercise: extension to three or more parallels (intercepts proportional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition III — Angle bisector theorem (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line (AD) bisect any angle (A) of a triangle (ABC), it divides the opposite side (BC) into segments proportional to the adjacent sides. Conversely, If the segments (BD, DC) into which a line (AD) drawn from any angle (A) of a triangle divides the opposite side be proportional to the adjacent sides, that line bisects the angle (A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by drawing through C a line parallel to AD meeting BA produced, then deducing equality of segments and proportions; exercises include external bisector, harmonic divisions, loci (circle giving ratio of sides), and various derived relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IV — Sides about equal angles of equiangular triangles are proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: The sides about the equal angles of equiangular triangles (BAC, CDE) are proportional, and those which are opposite to the equal angles are homologous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via constructing parallels or by superposition: placing one triangle onto the other so corresponding sides align and deducing parallelism and proportionality. Also remarks on lines meeting at infinity and parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition V — Sides proportional implies triangles equiangular
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have their sides proportional (BA:AC::ED:DF; AC:CB::DF:FE) they are equiangular, and those angles are equal which are subtended by the homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction proof: at D,E make angles equal to A,B then show triangles equiangular and equality of remaining sides; observation: this and previous proposition show equality of angles and proportionality are equivalent for triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VI — One angle equal and sides about it proportional => triangles equiangular
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have one angle (A) in one equal to one angle (D) in the other, and the sides about these angles proportional (BA:AC::ED:DF), the triangles are equiangular, and have those angles equal which are opposite to the homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to Proposition V via constructing appropriate points; includes Corollary: given ratio of two sides and included angle, the triangle is given in species (shape determined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VII — Similarity with species condition
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles (ABC, DEF) have one angle (A) one equal to one angle (D) in the other, the sides about two other angles (B, E) proportional (AB:BC::DE:EF), and the remaining angles (C, F) of the same species (i.e. either both acute or both not acute), the triangles are similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume unequal angles and construct segment leading to contradiction via 'species' condition; corollaries: if two sides proportional and one opposite angle equal then other opposite angles either equal or supplemental; if one right, other right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VIII — Altitude to hypotenuse produces similar triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: The triangles (ACD, BCD) into which a right-angled triangle (ACB) is divided, by the perpendicular (CD) from the right angle (C) on the hypotenuse, are similar to the whole and to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: CD is a mean proportional between AD and DB; BC is mean proportional between AB and BD; AC between AB and AD. Duplicate ratio relations: AD:DB :: AC²:CB², etc. Useful for constructing mean proportionals and relating segments in right triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IX — Problem: cut off a required submultiple of a line
rubrics_metrics.description: From a given right line (AB) to cut off any part required (i.e. to cut off any required submultiple).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw auxiliary line AF, mark equal parts on AF, join BF and draw parallel through the appropriate division to obtain the required submultiple on AB. General method for dividing a segment into any integer submultiple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition X — Divide a line similarly to a given divided line
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide a given undivided line (AB) similarly to a given divided line (CD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via drawing AG at an angle, copying partition lengths correspondingly on AG, joining BG and drawing parallels to BG to partition AB proportionally to CD. Corollaries: internal/external division in given ratio and harmonic division; various equivalent classical construction problems follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XI — Problem: find a third proportional to two given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a third proportional to two given lines (X, Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: on two rays form triangle with AB = X, BC = Y and AD = Y, draw BD and through C draw CE parallel to BD; then DE is third proportional such that X:Y = Y:DE. Alternative methods via Prop VIII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XII — Problem: find a fourth proportional to three given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a fourth proportional to three given lines (X, Y, Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction analogous to XI: take AB=X, BC=Y, AD=Z, draw BD and through C draw CE parallel to BD; then DE is fourth proportional (X:Y::Z:DE). Alternative via circle construction producing fourth proportional from intersecting chords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIII — Problem: find a mean proportional between two lines via semicircle
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a mean proportional between two given lines (X, Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: on AC set AB=X, BC=Y; describe semicircle on AC, erect BD perpendicular meeting semicircle at D; BD is mean proportional between AB and BC. Corollaries and alternative solutions via Prop VIII; many circle-based observations follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIV — Equiangular parallelograms area and reciprocal side proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Equiangular parallelograms (AB, CD) which are equal in area have the sides about the equal angles reciprocally proportional—AC:CE::GC:CB. 2. Equiangular parallelograms which have the sides about the equal angles reciprocally proportional are equal in area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses placing sides on a straight line and comparing ratios of sides and parallelograms; shows equivalence between reciprocal proportionality of adjacent sides and equality of area for equiangular parallelograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XV — Triangles equal in area and reciprocal proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Two triangles equal in area (ACB, DCE), which have one angle (C) in one equal to one angle (C) in the other, have the sides about these angles reciprocally proportional. 2. Two triangles, which have one angle in one equal to one angle in the other, and the sides about these angles reciprocally proportional, are equal in area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct analog of Prop XIV for triangles (halves of parallelograms); proofs by placing equal angles vertically opposite, joining diagonals and comparing ratios; useful when reasoning about area equality via side ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVI — Four proportional lines and rectangle equality
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. If four right lines (AB, CD, E, F) be proportional, the rectangle (AB·F) contained by the extremes is equal to the rectangle (CD·E) contained by the means. 2. If the rectangle contained by the extremes of four right lines be equal to the rectangle contained by the means, the four lines are proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: erect perpendiculars to form rectangles, use proportionality to deduce equality of constructed parallelograms/rectangles and converse. Alternative proof by putting lines concurrent and using cyclic quadrilateral product equality. Useful algebraic-geometry bridge: proportionality ⇔ product equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVII — Three proportional lines and square of the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. If three right lines (A, B, C) be proportional, the rectangle (A·C) contained by the extremes is equal to the square (B²) of the mean. 2. If the rectangle contained by the extremes of three right lines be equal to the square of the mean, the three lines are proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof derived from Prop XVI by setting D=B; basic identity: A:C = B²:AC etc. Corollary: fundamental relation used often in classical geometric mean problems; exercises show many geometric consequences combining with bisectors and circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVIII — Construct rectilineal figure similar to a given one on a given line
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given right line (AB) to construct a rectilineal figure similar to a given one (CDEFG), and similarly placed as regards any side (CD) of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: build successive triangles on AB, matching corresponding angles to generate a polygon ABHIJ similar to CDEFG. Observations: two figures (direct/inverse similarity) possible for each homologous side; corollaries on parallel homologous sides and construction by division in same ratio from a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIX — Areas of similar triangles are in duplicate ratio of homologous sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar triangles (ABC, DEF) have their areas to one another in the duplicate ratio of their homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses constructing a third proportional and reducing to equal-triangle comparison, or via squares on sides and comparing rectangles; duplicate ratio means square of ratio of homologous sides. Alternative proof provided for pedagogical clarity. Exercise: numerical area scaling when side lengths increase by a percentage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XX — Similar polygons: division into similar triangles and area ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar polygons may be divided (1) into the same number of similar triangles; (2) the corresponding triangles have the same ratio to one another which the polygons have; (3) the polygons are to each other in the duplicate ratio of their homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide polygons by diagonals from a vertex into triangles; apply Prop XIX to each corresponding triangle; gives area scaling for general similar polygons. Useful for area computations and scaling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation: equivalence of angle-equality and side-proportionality for triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: In VI. Def. i two conditions are laid down as necessary for the similitude of rectilineal figures. 1. The equality of angles; 2. The proportionality of sides. From Propositions IV and V, we see that if two triangles possess either condition, they also possess the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual rubric: for triangles, equality of angles and proportionality of sides are equivalent tests for similarity; important when deciding which criterion to apply in triangle similarity proofs (AA, SAS, SSS analogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises and corollaries as constructive/evaluative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the text many 'Exercises' and 'Cor.' items propose constructions and derived equalities (e.g., cutting lines in given ratios, harmonic divisions, mean proportional constructions, Ptolemy's theorem, relations for cyclic quadrilaterals, area identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises function as both practice constructions and as statements that must hold if preceding propositions are applied correctly. They serve as checks and extensions: use previous propositions, often involving parallels, cyclicity, and similar triangles, to derive results.
